_meta.purpose: Sourced religious-vocabulary catalog for the 11 prayer/time names and 5 explanation strings. Companion report: R6-PRAYER-NAME-CATALOG.md.

sourceSlugs.diyanet: Diyanet Isleri Baskanligi, namazvakitleri.diyanet.gov.tr (tr-TR and en-US pages)
sourceSlugs.kemenag: Kementerian Agama RI schedule criteria and the Indonesian imsakiyah convention it defines (bimasislam.kemenag.go.id)
sourceSlugs.jakim: JAKIM e-Solat label set, corroborated on mufti.pahang.gov.my/solat (Malaysia)
sourceSlugs.habous: Ministere des Habous et des Affaires Islamiques, habous.gov.ma (Morocco, French-language tables)
sourceSlugs.wikipedia-<lang>: Wikipedia in that language, article on salah/namaz
sourceSlugs.ml-wikipedia: ml.wikipedia.org Asr article and prayer navbox
sourceSlugs.ha-wikipedia: ha.wikipedia.org Sallar asuba / isha'i / la'asar articles
sourceSlugs.ru-wikipedia: ru.wikipedia.org Namaz article (Пятикратная ежедневная молитва table)
sourceSlugs.zh-wikipedia: zh.wikipedia.org 禮拜(伊斯蘭教) article; Taiwan religion.moi.gov.tw and PRC mzzjj.gz.gov.cn corroborate the five names
sourceSlugs.apple-so: Qur'aan Af-Soomaali App Store listing (Somali row names)
sourceSlugs.persian-usage: ordinary Persian religious usage, no single portal
sourceSlugs.nl-usage: ordinary Dutch Islamic-site usage, no single portal
sourceSlugs.derived: assembled from the sourced names of that language with standard syntax; not itself a citation
sourceSlugs.existing-app-catalog: already in shared/constants.ts of this repository

Fajr.note: Mihrab and al-azan agree. Diyanet's own Arabic-facing pages and KMSH's Arabic column use the same.

Sunrise.note: KMSH prints الشروق beside Lindja; al-azan uses the longer شروق الشمس. The short form is the standard table label.

Dhuhr.note: Also صلاة الظهر in full form.

Magrib.note: Arabic has the h; the English-only spelling Magrib is a Latin-script issue.

Midnight.note: Mihrab uses منتصف الليل. Both are current; نصف الليل matches the app's existing catalog. Iranian tables say نیمه شب شرعی (legal midnight), a Persian-only distinction.

Last Third.note: App catalog. The fuller phrasing is الثلث الأخير من الليل (Mihrab: الثلث الأخير). Either is defensible; keep app form for consistency.

Suhoor.note: AGPL catalog but also the ordinary Arabic word for the meal; dictionary-level certainty. Distinct from الإمساك, which is the deadline.

Duha.note: Quranic sura name, so dictionary-certain.

Istijaba.note: Stands for ساعة الاستجابة, the hour of answered supplication (islamqa.info 112165 uses وقت الاستجابة and الساعة الأخيرة من يوم الجمعة). Keep استجابة as the row label for length; the explanation string carries the full sense.

Start of the last third of the night.text: عند بداية الثلث الأخير من الليل

20 mins before Fajr.note: Arabic uses Arabic-Indic digits in some houses; Western digits are widely accepted. Verify digit shaping with the RTL plan (R3).

Fajr.note: Kemenag criteria and NU Online both print Subuh. Imsak is a separate earlier row (10 min before), never a synonym here. al-azan and Mihrab agree: Subuh.

Sunrise.note: jadwalsholat.org (Kemenag criteria) prints Terbit; NU Online prints Terbit; al-azan prints Terbit. Mihrab uses the longer Matahari terbit (16 chars) with abbreviation Terbt. Terbit alone is the standard table label.

Dhuhr.note: Spelling varies: Dzuhur (jadwalsholat.org, al-azan), Zuhur (NU Online), Dhuhur (Mihrab). All three read the same aloud. Dzuhur is the most common in Kemenag-derived tables.

Asr.note: Ashar (jadwalsholat.org, NU) vs Asar (al-azan, Mihrab). Both seen; Ashar is more common in Kemenag-derived tables.

Magrib.note: Indonesian keeps the h. All four Indonesian sources agree.

Isha.note: Sometimes Isya' with an apostrophe (NU, al-azan). Plain Isya is the cleaner table label.

Midnight.note: al-azan and Mihrab agree. No Kemenag table row exists; this is the ordinary Indonesian phrase.

Last Third.note: AGPL-only. The phrase is ordinary Indonesian (se pertiga, one third). Low legal risk but confirm with a speaker.

Suhoor.note: Universally Sahur in Indonesia. Imsak is the separate deadline row, exactly the distinction the app needs.

Duha.note: NU Online prints Dhuha as its own row between Terbit and Zuhur. jadwalsholat.org does too. Rare among authorities; Indonesia and Malaysia are the two that publish it.

Istijaba.note: Indonesian religious press says waktu istijabah for the Friday hour of answered dua (detik.com example). Not a standard table row anywhere. Consider leaving the Arabic-English form or dropping the row for id.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Assembled from the sourced name set and standard Indonesian syntax (antara X dan Y). Meaning-safe; have a speaker polish.

Start of the last third of the night.note: Derived from sepertiga akhir plus standard syntax.

20 mins before Fajr.note: menit (Jakarta usage) vs menit/menit; Kemenag tables say menit.

1 hour before Magrib (Fridays only).note: hari Jumat, standard Indonesian capitalization of day names.

Fajr.note: Urdu Wikipedia: نماز فجر. Tables print the bare name فجر; Mihrab and al-azan agree.

Sunrise.note: Mihrab and al-azan print it identically. The shorter طلوع also circulates. Do not use صبح صادق: that is true dawn, a different concept.

Dhuhr.note: Both catalogs agree.

Midnight.note: Mihrab. al-azan uses آدھی رات. Both are ordinary Urdu; نصف شب is the more formal table label.

Last Third.note: AGPL-only. Ordinary Urdu construction. Confirm with a speaker.

Suhoor.note: سحری is the meal; اختیارِ سحری / سحری کا وقت is the deadline. Pakistan tables print سحری for the meal row. Also called Sehri in roman Urdu.

Duha.note: No Urdu authority or catalog found that prints a Duha/Chasht row. The Arabic loanwword چاشت exists in religious prose (from Persian chasht). Recommend dropping the row for ur or keeping the Arabic الضحى.

Istijaba.note: No Urdu table or catalog found. Urdu religious prose says دعائیں قبول ہونے کی گھڑی (the hour when duas are accepted), a phrase, not a name. Recommend dropping the row for ur.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.text: مغرب اور فجر کے درمیان آدھی رات

Fajr.note: Bangladeshi tables print ফজর. Mihrab agrees; al-azan agrees.

Sunrise.note: Both catalogs agree; Bangladeshi papers use it. Astronomical register, as in English.

Dhuhr.note: Spelling varies: যোহর (muslimbangla, al-azan), জোহর (dhakapost), ধুহর (Mihrab). The যোহর/জোহর pair dominates Bangladeshi tables.

Asr.note: Also আছর in some papers. Both catalogs print আসর.

Magrib.note: All sources agree.

Isha.note: Also এশা in dhakapost. ইশা (al-azan, Mihrab) vs এশা (dhakapost): both widely seen.

Midnight.note: Mihrab and al-azan agree. Standard Bengali word.

Last Third.note: AGPL-only but ordinary Bengali (tritiyangsh, one third). Bangladeshi tables also say তাহাজ্জুদ for the same row.

Suhoor.note: muslimbangla prints সাহরী(শেষ) for the deadline; the meal is সাহরি/সেহরি. Mihrab prints সাহরি. Bangladeshi Ramadan calendars say সেহরি. Either সাহরি or সেহরি is correct; সেহরি is the common Ramadan-calendar form.

Duha.note: Bangladeshi nafil table prints চাশত (from Persian chasht) beside ইশরাক. The Arabic loan দোহা is rare in Bengali.

Istijaba.note: No Bengali table or catalog found. Bengali religious prose describes it, never names it in one word. Recommend dropping the row for bn.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Derived; মধ্যবর্তী is the standard Bengali for midway.

20 mins before Fajr.note: Bengali uses its own digits; verify rendering with the script plan (R3).

Fajr.note: THE trap. Diyanet's Turkish table prints İmsak where the English table prints Fajr (verified on both language versions of the same page, same times). İmsak is the fast's start, which Diyanet treats as the Fajr row label. Sabah is the prayer's name; Mihrab and al-azan split exactly this way (Mihrab: Sabah, al-azan: İmsak). Diyanet's own English page prints Fajr for the same instant.

Sunrise.note: Diyanet prints Güneş. Mihrab prints Gündoğumu (9 chars). Both current; Güneş is the Diyanet table label.

Dhuhr.note: All three sources agree.

Asr.note: All three agree.

Magrib.note: All three agree.

Isha.note: All three agree.

Midnight.note: Diyanet's own app and both catalogs print Gece yarısı.

Last Third.note: Turkish Islam names the last third by its prayer: Teheccüd (al-azan prints it; Diyanet TV uses it). A literal translation gecenin son üçte biri is a sentence, not a row label. shortText consideration: Teheccüd is the culturally correct row name.

Suhoor.note: Sahur is the meal (Mihrab). İmsak is its end. If Fajr is labelled İmsak, labelling Suhoor as Sahur is consistent and correct.

Duha.note: diyanethaber.com.tr: Duha veya işrak (kuşluk) namazı. Kuşluk is the Turkish name; İşrak is the rival term for the same 20-minute mark. Either works; Kuşluk is more common.

Istijaba.note: İsmail Ağa Camii materials call it İcâbet Saati. Not a Diyanet table row. Turkish convention writes it with a circumflex in older texts (İcâbet); modern spelling drops it.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Derived from Diyanet's own names; verify with a speaker.

Start of the last third of the night.note: al-azan's own hint string Teheccüd gecenin son üçte birlik kısmıdır attests every word of this.

20 mins before Fajr.note: Uses İmsak as the Fajr anchor, matching the row label. If the row is labelled İmsak this reads naturally.

20 mins after Sunrise.note: diyanethaber.com.tr describes the Duha time exactly this way (güneşin doğuşundan yaklaşık 20 dakika sonra).

Fajr.note: Habous prints Alfajr; the Grande Mosquée de Paris and mawaqit print Fajr. Mihrab agrees.

Sunrise.note: Habous prints Chourouq (the Arabic loan, 8 chars); Mihrab and mawaqit print Lever du soleil (16 chars). French Muslim usage is split. Chourouq is common in mosque calendars; Lever du soleil in apps. shortText: Chourouq.

Dhuhr.note: Habous prints Dhuhr. Dohr/Ad-dohr also seen (lematin.ma). Dhuhr is the app-neutral choice.

Asr.note: Habous prints Asr. Al-asr also seen.

Magrib.note: Habous prints Maghrib; Mihrab prints Maghreb (the French word for west/Morocco region). Mosques print Maghrib. Use Maghrib to keep the loanword distinct from the country name.

Isha.note: Habous prints Ishae; Mihrab prints Icha; mawaqit prints Isha. Isha is the neutral form.

Midnight.note: Mihrab. al-azan prints plain Minuit. The qualifier islamic disambiguates from 00:00; keep it. shortText: Minuit.

Last Third.note: AGPL-only but ordinary French.

Suhoor.note: Mihrab prints Souhour. French mosque calendars commonly write Sahour or Sohour. No authority prints it; pick Sahour and confirm.

Duha.note: No French authority or catalog found. French Muslim texts say prière du Duha or ad-Duha. Safest: keep the transliteration Duha.

Istijaba.note: No French table or catalog found. French fatwa sites describe l'heure d'exaucement du vendredi, a phrase. Recommend dropping the row for fr or shipping the transliteration Istijaba.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.text: À mi-chemin entre Maghrib et Fajr
Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Derived; standard French syntax.

Start of the last third of the night.text: Début du dernier tiers de la nuit

20 mins before Fajr.note: French abbreviates minutes as min.

20 mins after Sunrise.text: 20 min après le lever du soleil

Fajr.note: German-Islamic usage: Fadschr (al-azan, gebetszeiten.de) or Fajr (Mihrab). Fadschr is the German transliteration standard (dsch for j); Fajr is also common in mosque calendars. Both defensible; Fajr is shorter and matches the app's other languages.

Sunrise.note: Both catalogs print Sonnenaufgang. gebetszeiten.de uses the Arabic loan Schuruk for the row. Sonnenaufgang is the plain-German label; Schuruk is the community label.

Dhuhr.note: Mihrab Dhuhr; al-azan Zuhr; gebetszeiten.de Dhuhr. Dhuhr dominates German mosque calendars.

Asr.note: Mihrab and gebetszeiten.de print Asr. al-azan prints Nachmittagsgebet (19 chars), the translated concept.

Magrib.note: Mihrab and gebetszeiten.de print Maghrib. al-azan prints Abendgebet (evening prayer), the translated concept.

Isha.note: German transliteration: Ischa (al-azan), Isha (Mihrab). German orthography writes sch for sh, so Ischa is the German-standard form; Isha is also widespread.

Midnight.note: Both catalogs print Mitternacht. Mihrab's fuller Islamische Mitternacht (21 chars) disambiguates; plain Mitternacht is the row label.

Last Third.note: Mihrab; al-azan's hint string attestiert das letzte Drittel der Nacht.

Suhoor.note: Mihrab. German Ramadan calendars say Suhur or Sahur. No authority source.

Duha.note: No German authority or catalog found. German texts say Duha-Gebet or Morgengebet (which more often means Fajr). Recommend keeping the transliteration Duha.

Istijaba.note: No German table or catalog found. German fatwa sites describe die Stunde der Erhörung am Freitag, a phrase. Recommend dropping the row for de.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Derived; halbwegs zwischen is more colloquial. Confirm.

Start of the last third of the night.text: Beginn des letzten Drittels der Nacht
Start of the last third of the night.note: Every word attested in al-azan's German hint string.

20 mins before Fajr.note: German abbreviates Minuten as Min.

Fajr.note: Iranian tables print اذان صبح (badesaba, tala, tabdil). The bare word فجر is the Quranic name (al-azan prints it). اذان صبح is the row label users expect; فجر is the short form.

Sunrise.note: All Iranian portals agree. al-azan prints the shorter طلوع. Either works; طلوع آفتاب is the full table label.

Dhuhr.note: Iranian tables print اذان ظهر; the bare form is ظهر (al-azan).

Asr.note: badesaba lists اذان عصر; some portals omit this row and print only غروب آفتاب next. Attested.

Magrib.note: Iranian tables distinguish غروب آفتاب (sunset) from اذان مغرب (the prayer, some minutes later). The app's single Magrib row is the prayer, so اذان مغرب is correct.

Isha.note: Bare form عشاء (al-azan). Iranian convention writes عشا without hamza.

Midnight.note: All Iranian portals print نیمه شب شرعی (legal midnight). The qualifier شرعی is mandatory in Persian to distinguish from 00:00 clock midnight.

Last Third.note: al-azan's Persian hint: تهجد ثلث آخر شب است. Iranian sites also say آخر شب for the same instant. ثلث آخر شب is precise.

Suhoor.note: Persian religious press uses سحری for the meal. No portal prints a سحری row outside Ramadan. The deadline is اذان صبح, so the split matches the app's Suhoor-vs-Fajr distinction.

Duha.note: Persian religious press: نماز چاشت یا ضحی. چاشت (from Persian chasht) is the Iranian name; ضحی is the Arabic loan. Either works.

Istijaba.note: No Persian portal prints it. Shia sources place the Friday answered-hour differently, so the Saudi-fixed definition may not suit the Iranian calendar anyway. Recommend dropping the row for fa.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.text: نیمه شب بین مغرب و صبح

Fajr.note: JAKIM e-Solat label set, verified on mufti.pahang.gov.my (JAKIM data): Subuh. MUIS Singapore uses Subuh too. Imsak is the separate earlier row (10 min), never a synonym.

Sunrise.note: JAKIM prints Syuruk (also spelled Syuruq). The astronomical alternative is Matahari terbit; Syuruk is the standard Malaysian table label.

Dhuhr.note: JAKIM prints Zohor (also Zuhr/Dhuhr in some Malaysian apps). MUIS prints Zohor.

Asr.note: JAKIM prints Asar; also spelled Asar/Ashar. Mihrab's id locale uses Asar for the same concept.

Magrib.note: JAKIM and MUIS print Maghrib.

Isha.note: JAKIM prints Isyak; MUIS prints Isyak. (Indonesian is Isya; the k is the Malaysian marker.)

Midnight.note: Malaysian apps print Tengah malam. No JAKIM row. Ordinary Malay phrase, same as Indonesian.

Last Third.note: No authority or catalog found for ms specifically. Indonesian Sepertiga akhir (Mihrab) plus malam is the obvious Malay construction; needs a speaker.

Suhoor.note: Malaysian Ramadan calendars universally print Sahur; Imsak is the separate deadline row in JAKIM's set.

Duha.note: JAKIM-family tables print Dhuha as its own row between Syuruk and Zohor (verified: mufti.pahang.gov.my). Malaysia and Indonesia are the two authorities that publish it.

Istijaba.note: No Malaysian table or catalog found. Malay religious press says waktu mustajab (the accepted time) for the Friday hour. Recommend dropping the row or using Waktu mustajab after speaker review.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Derived; standard Malay syntax.

Start of the last third of the night.note: Derived; same caveat as the name.

Fajr.note: Swahili Wikishia and the bongoclass hadith translation both use Alfajiri. Note bongoclass spells it Alfajir; Alfajiri (the dawn) is the standard Swahili word. al-azan keeps Fajr. East African mosque calendars print Alfajiri.

Sunrise.note: al-azan prints Macheo (also tama). Standard Swahili for sunrise. al-azan's Swahili midnight string confirms machweo (sunset) vs macheo (sunrise) distinction: Machweo hadi Macheo.

Dhuhr.note: Swahili Wikishia prints Adhuhuri; bongoclass prints Adhuhuri. Also Dhuhur. The doubled form with the Arabic article (Ad-) is the Swahili convention: Adhuhuri, Alasiri, Magharibi.

Asr.note: Wikishia prints Alasiri; bongoclass prints Al'asiri/Alasiri. Standard Swahili afternoon-prayer name.

Magrib.note: Wikishia prints Magharibi; bongoclass prints Magharibi. al-azan prints Magharibi. Same word as the Swahili compass direction (west), so it reads naturally.

Isha.note: Wikishia prints Isha; bongoclass prints Ishai. Both seen; Isha matches the app's English.

Midnight.note: al-azan prints Katikati ya usiku (middle of the night).

Last Third.note: al-azan's hint string: Tahajjud ni theluthi ya mwisho ya usiku. Attested verbatim.

Suhoor.note: No Swahili authority or catalog found for the meal row. Swahili Ramadan usage says mlo wa usiku wa manane or the Arabic Suhur. Recommend keeping the transliteration Suhur after speaker review.

Duha.note: No Swahili authority or catalog found. The Arabic loan Duha is used in Swahili religious radio. Keep the transliteration Duha.

Istijaba.note: No Swahili table or catalog found. Swahili describes it as saa ya maombi kukubalika Ijumaa. Recommend dropping the row for sw.

Fajr.note: islamhouse Hausa and Hausa Wikipedia: Sallar asuba (dawn prayer). Bare form Asuba works as the row label; Hausa convention is Sallar X (the prayer of X).

Sunrise.note: islamhouse uses fitowar rana repeatedly (sunrise) as the boundary of the dawn prayer. Astronomical register, not a prayer name.

Dhuhr.note: islamhouse and Hausa Wikipedia: Azahar. Hausa keeps the Persian-derived name (from zuhr via Persian).

Asr.note: Hausa Wikipedia calls it La'asar (also Sallar La'asar); islamhouse prose says la'asar. Asora appears in Hausa Islamic lists. La'asar is the more common Hausa name; category pages use both.

Magrib.note: Hausa Wikipedia article title is Maghrib with prose Magrib; the Hausa form is Magriba or La'asar rinjeya. Northern Nigerian calendars print Magriba.

Isha.note: Hausa Wikipedia: Sallar isha'i. The apostrophe is part of the spelling.

Midnight.note: No Hausa table found printing a midnight row. Hausa says tsakar dare (midnight). Not attested in an Islamic-time context; needs a speaker.

Last Third.note: No Hausa source found for the last-third concept. Tahajjud is the name used in Hausa religious radio. Needs a speaker.

Suhoor.note: Hausa Ramadan usage says azumin rana with the pre-dawn meal called shan izza or sallar asuba time. Not attested as a table row. Needs a speaker.

Duha.note: No Hausa source found. The Arabic loan Duha appears in Hausa religious audio. Needs a speaker.

Istijaba.note: No Hausa source found. Recommend dropping the row for ha.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Needs the name set confirmed first.

Fajr.note: Somali mosque page (masjidbox, ISWA) prints Subax. Somali tawkit.net mirror prints Subax. The Arabic loan Fajr also circulates; Subax is the Somali word.

Sunrise.note: masjidbox prints Waaberi for the sunrise row. Also qorrax soobaxa (sun rising) in Somali tables. Waaberi is the compact table label.

Dhuhr.note: masjidbox prints Duhur; tawkit prints Dhuhr.

Asr.note: masjidbox prints Casar; tawkit prints Casr. Casar is the fuller Somali form.

Magrib.note: masjidbox prints Maqrib; tawkit prints Maghrib. Somali drops the gh for q; Maqrib is the Somali spelling.

Isha.note: masjidbox prints Cishaa'i (with the Somali c for ayn). Apostrophe is part of the spelling.

Midnight.note: Ordinary Somali for midnight is hora hose/habeen dhexe. Not attested in an Islamic-time table. Needs a speaker.

Last Third.note: Not found. Somali religious audio uses Tahajjud. Needs a speaker.

Suhoor.note: The Somali Qur'aan Af-Soomaali app listing shows Sahri among its row names (Apple App Store). Single app source; also needs a better slug registered if promoted.

Duha.note: Same Somali app listing shows Duha (Chast). Single app source.

Istijaba.note: No Somali source found. Recommend dropping the row for so.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Needs the name set confirmed first.

Fajr.note: ps.wikipedia describes د سهار د لمانځه وخت. islamery.ps prints the Arabic loan صبح for the row. Two conventions: Arabic loan (فجر/صبح) or Pashto phrase. Tables prefer the short loan.

Sunrise.note: ps.islamery prints لمرختنه for the sunrise row. Attested exactly.

Dhuhr.note: islamery prints غرمې لمونځ. The bare time word is غرمې.

Asr.note: islamery prints ماسپښين لمونځ. Note: Pashto ماسپښين means afternoon; مازديګر (from Persian) is the rival term for the same prayer. Tables use either.

Magrib.note: islamery prints ماښام لمونځ. From Persian khwab-maaz; means evening.

Isha.note: islamery prints ماسخوتن لمونځ (note the o vs kh variance: ماسخوتن/ماسختن both appear). Also عشاء kept in Arabic script.

Midnight.note: No Pashto table row found. Pashto says د شپې نيمه. Needs a speaker.

Last Third.note: No Pashto source found for the row. Tahajjud is the circulating name. Needs a speaker.

Suhoor.note: Pashto Ramadan calendars say سهاري (sahari). Not attested in a table I could read. Needs a speaker.

Duha.note: No Pashto source found. Recommend keeping the Arabic الضحى or dropping.

Istijaba.note: No Pashto source found. Recommend dropping the row for ps.

Halfway between Magrib and Fajr.note: Needs the name set confirmed first.

Fajr.note: ku.wikipedia (Kurmanji) Nimêj table: Sibe. Alternative: dema sibê. Turkish-influenced Kurmanji speakers say Sabah (from Turkish); Sibe is the Kurmanji word.

Sunrise.note: ku.wikipedia attests derketina rojê (rising of the sun) in prose. No table row found. Kurmanji also uses Rojhilat (east, where the sun rises) loosely for the morning prayer, which is ambiguous. Needs a speaker.

Dhuhr.note: ku.wikipedia table: Nîvro.

Asr.note: ku.wikipedia table: Esir / Piştî Nivro.

Fajr.note: islom.uz prints Бомдод (Cyrillic) / Bomdod (Latin). Also Tong (dawn) on praytime.uz. Bomdod is the canonical Uzbek name; Tong is praytime.uz's label for the same row.

Suhoor.note: islom.uz annotates Bomdod with Saharlik (the fast-start). namozvaqti.uz prints Saharlik as its own row label. The meal itself is saharlik ovqati; the deadline word is Saharlik. For the app's Suhoor row (deadline convention), Saharlik is correct.

Duha.note: islom.uz prints Ишроқ as its own row and defines it exactly as the app defines Duha: 20 minutes after sunrise (Кун чиққандан сўнг 20 дақиқа ўтгач). This is the best authority match for Duha in any language.

Suhoor.note: Tamil Ramadan calendars say நோன்பு உணவு (fast food, literally) or the Arabic Sahar. Not attested in a table I could read. Needs a speaker.
